catalog_quote: (1) There is no tone sandhi phenomenon. [p. 4] ... The vowel /ə/ occurs only when the vowel /a/ is destressed under neutral tone. Thus /iāt/ 'one' becomes /iə̄t/ when destressed and under neutral tone. [p. 6] ... I.1.3. Tones. Xuwen has five open-syllable tones and two closed syllable tones. [chart: Open 55, 33, 11, 24, 42; Closed 5, 1] The low level tone has a low falling 21 variant in phrase-final position. No systematic tone sandhi was found. A few words, however, display free variations between two tones ... [pp. 7-8] ... The tone marking conventions used in this paper are the following: a. High level tones are marked with a macron high above the main vowel ... e. Neutral tone in unmarked. [p. 8, sic] ... /lo/ alternating with unstressed /lo/ is shown functioning as a durative aspect marker in the following examples: [p. 16] ... The nominalizing particle is /kâi/ which also occurs in the genitive phrase ... It can be reduced to [e] or [ae] in normal-speed speech where the particle is typically destressed. [p. 19]

new_statements.rule_in_words: The source gives no rule for where word stress falls. It describes Xuwen (Leizhou Min) as a tone language with five open-syllable tones (55, 33, 11, 24, 42) and two checked-syllable tones (5, 1) and no tone sandhi; syllables can be 'destressed', in which case they carry a neutral (toneless, unmarked) tone and their vowel /a/ reduces to /ə/. The destressed elements exemplified are the numeral 'one' in compound numerals and grammatical particles (aspect marker /lo/ 'unstressed', nominalizer /kai/ 'typically destressed' in normal-speed speech). Tone, not stress, is the lexically contrastive prosody; stress is only mentioned as the loss of tone on reduced syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: None concerning stress; a few words show free variation between two tones (e.g. 'middle', 'fragrant', 'head', 'old', p. 8).
new_statements.domain_note: Word and phrase: destressing is shown on the second element of a compound numeral ('one' inside 'eleven', 'seventy-one') and on clitic-like particles in connected speech; citation forms carry full lexical tone. Data from one speaker (Mrs Deng Yongni, Xuwen county, elicited in Hong Kong 1981).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes the Xuwen (徐闻) county dialect at the southern tip of the Leizhou Peninsula, from a single speaker who left Xuwen in the 1960s (elicited in Hong Kong, 1981). Glottolog has no separate code for Xuwen; it falls under leiz1236 Leizhou Chinese. Li & Thompson classify it as Southern Min (their French abstract calls it a Min-Yue mixture) and note that its lack of tone sandhi is unusual within Min, so the 雷城/Suixi varieties described by Zhang & Cai 1998 and Yue-Hashimoto 1985 may differ prosodically. The Chen 2023 paper describes the Leizhou variety spoken in Malaysia, not the homeland.

sources.note: Phonology section I.1 (pp. 4-9): 'There is no tone sandhi phenomenon' (p. 4); five open-syllable tones (55, 33, 11, 24, 42) and two checked tones (5, 1), 'No systematic tone sandhi was found' (p. 7); a neutral tone exists and is left unmarked (p. 8); '/ə/ occurs only when the vowel /a/ is destressed under neutral tone' with 'one' /iāt/ > /iə̄t/ (p. 6); in the grammar section the aspect particle /lo/ appears 'unstressed' and the nominalizer /kai/ is 'typically destressed' in normal-speed speech (pp. 16-17). No rule for where word stress falls.
